unit.title: The Future Subjunctive
unit.subtitle: Hablare, fuere and the frozen -re forms of law and proverb

grammar.title: The tense that almost died
grammar.intro: The future subjunctive (hablare, tuviere, fuere) once expressed a hypothetical future, but in modern Spanish it is virtually extinct in speech. It survives only in legal texts, proverbs, and a handful of frozen expressions. A C2 speaker doesn't produce it freely — you recognise it, read it as roughly the present subjunctive, and know it belongs to those set contexts only.

sections.heading: How the -re forms are built
sections.body: Take the third-person plural preterite (hablaron, tuvieron, fueron), drop -ron, and add -re, -res, -re, -remos, -reis, -ren. So it shares its irregular stem with the imperfect subjunctive — tuviera ↔ tuviere, fuera ↔ fuere. There is a compound form too: hubiere hablado.
conj: hablare, hablares, hablare, habláremos, hablareis, hablaren

ex.es: El que infringiere esta norma será sancionado.
ex.en: Whoever breaks this rule shall be penalised.

ex.es: Si alguien lo supiere, que lo declare.
ex.en: Should anyone know it, let them declare it.

sections.heading: Proverbs and frozen expressions
sections.body: A small set of fixed phrases keeps the future subjunctive alive in everyday cultural memory. They mean roughly “whatever may happen / wherever you may go”. You use them as blocks; you don't conjugate new verbs into them.
conj: Be that as it may / whatever it may be
Adonde fueres, haz lo que vieres
When in Rome, do as the Romans do

ex.es: Sea lo que fuere, no pienso rendirme.
ex.en: Whatever may come, I don't intend to give up.
Wherever you go, do as you see (When in Rome…).
ex.note: a proverb, learned as a block

sections.heading: Register: recognise it, don't overuse it
sections.body: The future subjunctive signals legal or archaic-solemn register. In modern prose or speech you would use the present subjunctive instead: everyday Spanish says el que lo sepa, and only a statute would write el que lo supiere. Producing it in casual contexts sounds either legalistic or affectedly old-fashioned — the C2 skill is knowing when not to use it.
conj: El que lo sepa, que lo diga
El que lo supiere, que lo declare

ex.es: En el habla real diríamos “pase lo que pase”, no “viniere”.
ex.en: In real speech we'd say “pase lo que pase”, not “viniere”.
ex.note: present subj. is the living form

ex.es: Solo un texto jurídico escribe “quien incumpliere el contrato…”.
ex.en: Only a legal text writes “whoever breaches the contract…”.

takeaways: Future subjunctive endings: -re, -res, -re, -remos, -reis, -ren, on the preterite stem (fueron → fuere).
It survives only in legal language, proverbs, and frozen phrases like ‘sea lo que fuere’.
In meaning it equals the present subjunctive: el que infringiere ≈ el que infrinja.
The C2 skill is to recognise it and NOT overuse it — modern Spanish prefers the present subjunctive.

mistakes.why: In ordinary speech the future subjunctive is dead; use the present subjunctive: cuando llegues.

mistakes.w: Sea lo que sea… (quoting the proverb) → but written as ‘sea lo que fuera’.
mistakes.why: The fixed proverb keeps the future subjunctive fuere; ‘fuera’ breaks the set expression.

mistakes.w: El que infringe la norma será sancionado. (in a statute)
mistakes.r: El que infringiere la norma será sancionado.
mistakes.why: In legal register the future subjunctive (infringiere) is the expected, formulaic choice.

exercises.prompt: En un contrato: “El que ___ esta cláusula responderá de los daños.”
exercises.prompt_en: In a contract: “Whoever breaches this clause shall be liable for damages.”
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! El registro jurídico usa el futuro de subjuntivo: infringiere.
exercises.no: Legal texts use the future subjunctive here: “El que infringiere esta cláusula…” (= infrinja).

exercises.prompt: El futuro de subjuntivo “fuere” equivale en significado a…
exercises.prompt_en: In meaning, the future subjunctive “fuere” is equivalent to…
exercises.ok: ¡Exacto! El futuro de subjuntivo se lee como presente de subjuntivo.
exercises.no: In meaning the future subjunctive equals the present subjunctive: fuere ≈ sea.

exercises.prompt: Build the saying: “Whatever may come, I won't give up.”
exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! “Sea lo que fuere” es una fórmula fija.
exercises.no: The frozen phrase keeps the future subjunctive: “Sea lo que fuere, no pienso rendirme.”

exercises.prompt: Refrán: “Adonde fueres, haz lo que ___.” (ver, futuro de subjuntivo)
exercises.prompt_en: Proverb: “Wherever you go, do as you see” (When in Rome…).
exercises.hint: Future subjunctive of ver, rhyming with 'fueres'.
exercises.no: The proverb is “Adonde fueres, haz lo que vieres” — future subjunctive of ver.

exercises.prompt: Match each frozen expression to its English meaning.
pairs: Adonde fueres, haz lo que vieres
exercises.ok: ¡Excelente! Reconoces el -re en su hábitat natural.

exercises.tts: Sea lo que fuere, seguiremos adelante.
accepted: sea lo que fuere seguiremos adelante
exercises.translation: Whatever may be, we'll carry on.
exercises.no: It was: “Sea lo que fuere, seguiremos adelante.”

lines.speaker: Nacho
lines.es: Oye, cuando llegues a casa, ¿me avisas?
lines.en: Hey, when you get home, will you let me know?

options.text: Claro, en cuanto llegue te escribo.
Claro, en cuanto llegare te escribo.
Claro, en cuanto llegaré te escribo.

exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! En el habla real: presente de subjuntivo, no el futuro de subjuntivo.
exercises.no: Everyday speech uses the present subjunctive: “en cuanto llegue”, never the archaic llegare.

exercises.say: Sea lo que fuere, no pienso rendirme.
exercises.en: Whatever may come, I don't intend to give up.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the rhythm of “Sea lo que fuere, no pienso rendirme.”
